title: Symmetry Classification of Non-Reciprocal Responses in Multiterminal Ring Devices
abstract: We present a symmetry-based framework to classify the non-reciprocal responses of multiterminal ring quantum devices. The device is modeled as a ring of $n$ vertices, where a binary variable $e_k\in\{+1,-1\}$ on each bond encodes the preferred direction of signal flow between terminals. Non-reciprocity corresponds to a preferred current configuration on the ring, and the symmetry group of the device partitions all $2^n$ configurations into equivalence classes(orbits) characterized by a topological winding number $W$. Using the minimal non-trivial case $n=3$, we establish two results independent of microscopic details. First, lifting the degeneracy within an orbit generates non-reciprocal responses. For $n=3$ this requires simultaneous breaking of both time-reversal $T$ and spatial inversion $I$. Breaking either alone is insufficient. Second, the residual geometry symmetry after $T$ and $I$ are broken determines which responses are observable. For an isosceles triangular geometry, only two types of response are allowed: uniform circulation (all bonds carrying current in the same direction) and semi-circulation with the reversed bond on the geometrically distinct base. Semi-circulation with the reversed bond on either equal leg is symmetry-forbidden. Both predictions are validated using a minimal toy model of three quantum dots coupled to superconducting baths, which demonstrates a reactive quantum circulator response.
summary: This paper introduces a group-theoretic framework to classify non-reciprocal current responses in quantum ring devices. Using symmetry analysis on $n$-vertex rings, the authors predict that observable non-reciprocity requires breaking both time-reversal and inversion symmetries simultaneously. The theory is validated using a three-site superconducting quantum dot model, confirming predictions for circulator and semi-circulator transport regimes.
main_problem: The paper develops a symmetry-based framework to classify non-reciprocal responses occurring in multiterminal quantum ring devices.
main_result: Non-reciprocity requires the simultaneous breaking of both time-reversal (T) and spatial inversion (I) symmetries. The geometry dictates which specific circulator or semi-circulator responses are physically observable.
method: The analysis heavily relies on group theory, specifically applying Burnside's Lemma to classify the $2^n$ possible current configurations into symmetry equivalence classes (orbits).
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a ring of $n$ vertices with bonds characterized by preferred signal flow directions ($\pm 1$). The theoretical predictions are validated using a minimal toy model of three quantum dots coupled to superconducting baths.
key_observables: Non-reciprocal transmission ($S_{nr}$), the reactive component of the current-current response function ($	ext{Im}[\chi_{nr}]$), and the absolute non-reciprocal weight ($R_{nr}^{tot}$).
important_parameters: The number of terminals $n$ (especially $n=3$), geometric symmetry (equilateral vs. isosceles), and external fields like Zeeman field ($b_y$) or SOC ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the non-reciprocal response can be entirely classified by the underlying discrete symmetries of the ring geometry, even when microscopic details are involved.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $n$-vertex ring setup and show examples of circulator ($W=3$) and semi-circulator ($W=1$) configurations. Other figures plot non-reciprocal transmission spectra, reactive response functions ($	ext{Im}[\chi_{nr}]$), and energy level splittings as a function of symmetry breaking parameters.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general group theory framework for $n$-rings to analyzing specific cases ($n=3$ equilateral vs. isosceles) using Burnside's lemma, culminating in validation via calculations on a minimal quantum dot toy model that predicts observable circulator and semi-circulator responses.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool—symmetry classification—to predict fundamental transport properties (non-reciprocity) in mesoscopic superconducting circuits, linking topology/geometry directly to measurable electrical response.
